extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers seeking practical/philosophical guidance on self-governance (readers of Montaigne)
extracted.subtask_description: A reflective early-modern personal essay giving practical maxims for managing one's will, passions, desires, and public engagement; combines moral prescriptions, examples, and rhetorical observations. Useful as guidance on how to live moderately and preserve inner liberty while engaging with society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate insensibility to be moved by few things
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Tis but reason they should concern a man, provided they do not possess him; I am very solicitous ... to enlarge this privilege of insensibility ... so that consequently I espouse and am very much moved with very few things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop a disposition to feel but not be possessed by external events (even health); fix your attention on few objects and avoid letting things wholly possess you. Practical aim: be concerned without being possessed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderate between hatred of pain and love of pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: A man ought to moderate himself betwixt the hatred of pain and the love of pleasure: and Plato sets down a middle path of life betwixt the two.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the ‘middle path’ — avoid extremes of seeking pleasure or escaping pain; temper desires so they do not overwhelm judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lend yourself to others but give yourself to yourself
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Tis my opinion that a man should lend himself to others, and only give himself to himself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When serving others, do so without surrendering your inner liberty or identity; accept duties but do not incorporate others' affairs into your very being.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be thrifty of the liberty of your soul
rubrics_metrics.description: We must be thrifty of the liberty of our souls, and never let it out but upon just occasions, which are very few, if we judge aright.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protect your mental freedom: avoid being at everyone’s call or spreading attention thinly. Reserve time and will for important matters only.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid occupation-for-its-own-sake
rubrics_metrics.description: Occupation, with a certain sort of men, is a mark of understanding and dignity: their souls seek repose in agitation ... No one distributes his money to others, but every one distributes his time and his life: there is nothing of which we are so prodigal as of these two things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not mistake constant busyness for virtue. Conserve time and life; avoid throwing yourself into unnecessary public bustle because it confers status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Act without passion; keep the bridle in your hand
rubrics_metrics.description: To be simply acting costs him so little, that he acts even sleeping; but it must be set on going with discretion ... he always marches with the bridle in his hand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carry out duties calmly, without vexation or passion. Let judgement, not impetuosity, govern actions so you can recover and retry without being undone by emotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use judgement and address rather than impetuous desire
rubrics_metrics.description: He who therein employs only his judgment and address proceeds more cheerfully ... In him who is intoxicated with this violent and tyrannical intention, we discover ... much imprudence and injustice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor prudence, flexibility, and strategy over violent, single-minded zeal; impetuosity leads to poor results and injustice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit engagement with public office and honors
rubrics_metrics.description: I entreated to be excused [as mayor]; ... ‘Tis an office that ought to be looked upon so much more honourable, as it has no other salary nor advantage than the bare honour of its execution ... I should be very sorry anything should make so great an impression upon me as their affairs ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of public roles that will intrude on personal life and health; accept offices only when they do not compromise your inner tranquillity or private duties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strip yourself of choler to make chastisement better
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophy directs that, in the revenge of injuries received, we should strip ourselves of choler; not that the chastisement should be less, but ... that the revenge may be the better and more heavily laid on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Control anger when seeking redress so your actions are more effective; passion weakens the executor of punishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize self-defeating nature of excessive passion (haste trips)
rubrics_metrics.description: In precipitation, “festinatio tarda est,”--haste trips up its own heels ... Impetus manages all things ill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Know that excess speed and ardor often undermine outcomes; adopt measured pace to avoid self-entanglement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish natural desires from products of fancy; limit desires to what is visible
rubrics_metrics.description: They very subtly distinguish betwixt the desires that proceed from [nature], and those that proceed from the disorder of our own fancy: those of which we can see the end are hers; those that fly before us, and of which we can see no end, are our own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept and satisfy natural needs (those with observable ends) but curb limitless fanciful desires that have no clear end; this mitigates exposure to Fortune.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer a small sufficiency; patience is central
rubrics_metrics.description: Of so many parts as make up a sufficiency, patience is the most sufficient. ... If that which nature exactly and originally requires of us ... be too little ... let us allow ourselves a little more ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for sufficiency rather than excess; cultivate patience as a key virtue for contentment and resilience to fortune.

rubrics_metrics.name: Custom is a second nature; resist radical late-life change
rubrics_metrics.description: Custom is a second nature, and no less powerful. ... I am no longer in condition for any great change, nor to put myself into a new and unwonted course ... It is past the time for me to become other than what I am.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge the force of long habit; do not expect abrupt, wholesale reformation late in life; temper expectations about personal change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderate emotions even in trivial activities (games)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider, that even in vain and frivolous actions, as at chess, tennis ... this eager and ardent engaging with an impetuous desire, immediately throws the mind and members into indiscretion and disorder ... the less peevish and passionate he is at play, he plays much more advantageously and surely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply calm moderation even in play; passion undermines performance in both trivial and serious affairs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not incorporate others' affairs into your very being
rubrics_metrics.description: If, sometimes, I have been put upon the management of other men’s affairs, I have promised to take them in hand, but not into my lungs and liver; to take them upon me, not to incorporate them; to take pains, yes: to be impassioned about it, by no means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take responsibility without allowing others' problems to consume your inner life; preserve separation between your identity and external duties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep desires circumscribed; avoid actions that run before oneself
rubrics_metrics.description: The career of our desires ought to be circumscribed and restrained to a short limit of the nearest and most contiguous commodities; ... Actions that are carried on without this reflection ... such actions ... are erroneous and sickly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constrain ambitions and acquisitiveness to avoid exposing oneself unduly to fortune and adversity; prefer aims that return you to yourself rather than propel you away.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be your own friend to better serve others
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Qui sibi amicus est, scito hunc amicum omnibus esse.’ — He who is his own friend, is a friend to everybody else.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By attending properly to your own conduct and duties to yourself, you become better positioned to fulfill obligations to others; self-care is a prerequisite for public service.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prudently apply sages’ precepts; be aware they may be prescriptive, not factual
rubrics_metrics.description: Most of the rules and precepts of the world run this way; to drive us out of ourselves into the street for the benefit of public society; they thought to do a great feat to divert and remove us from ourselves, assuming we were but too much fixed there, and by a too natural inclination; and have said all they could to that purpose: for ’tis no new thing for the sages to preach things as they serve, not as they are.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat universal precepts with pragmatic caution: recognize that some moral precepts aim to induce behaviour rather than describe human nature; apply them judiciously rather than blindly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Play your social role but do not make the mask your substance
rubrics_metrics.description: We must play our part properly, but withal as a part of a borrowed personage; we must not make real essence of a mask and outward appearance; nor of a strange person, our own; we cannot distinguish the skin from the shirt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fulfill social roles when required, but avoid conflating outward role/appearance with your true self; maintain inner authenticity despite public performance.
